questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why death rates rose in nineteenth-century industrial towns
questions.stem: A transit planner's board reviews a cholera outbreak in an industrial town where wells sit beside open drains. Which factor most directly worsened mortality?

options.text: Contaminated water supplies mingling with human waste
The export of surplus grain to continental markets
options.misconception: blames a trade pattern unrelated to local water quality

options.text: The town's rapid population growth without matching sewer investment
options.misconception: confuses population size with the actual transmission route

options.text: The arrival of railway lines through the town center
options.misconception: mistakes transport infrastructure for a disease vector

questions.explanation: Cholera spread through water contaminated by sewage, so the direct cause was polluted supplies. Population pressure mattered only by overwhelming sanitation, and railways or grain exports did not transmit the disease.
questions.hint: Trace the disease from waste to mouth.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain a shift from iron to steel production
questions.stem: A transit planner's board asks why the second wave of industry favored steel over iron for railways and ships. Provide a model answer.

answer.exemplar: Steel could be produced more cheaply and in larger quantities after new processes removed impurities from iron, and its greater strength and durability made it superior for rails, bridges, and hulls. Iron remained useful but could not match steel's performance at scale.

questions.explanation: The Bessemer and open-hearth processes lowered costs while improving quality, so steel displaced iron in heavy construction. Earlier iron technology lacked both the scale and the strength required.
questions.hint: Name the process and the property gained.

questions.learningObjective: Explain a limitation of the 1848 Act
questions.stem: A transit planner's board asks why the 1848 Act failed to transform most towns immediately. Provide a model answer.

questions.explanation: Voluntary adoption and local cost fears limited uptake. The Act created powers but not obligations, so compulsion arrived only with subsequent laws.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a source on water supply reform

stimulus.body: After the 1854 cholera outbreak, a local board closed a contaminated pump and redirected households to a cleaner source. Deaths fell sharply within weeks. Neighboring districts that delayed action saw no comparable decline.

questions.stem: A transit planner's board reads this source. What does it best support?

options.text: Closing pumps caused cholera
Cholera declined naturally everywhere
options.misconception: ignores the contrast with delaying districts

options.text: Clean water intervention reduced cholera deaths
Delayed action was equally effective

questions.explanation: The source shows deaths fell where water was cleaned and not where action was delayed. It supports intervention effectiveness, not natural decline or pump-caused disease.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Synthesize the Act's legacy
questions.stem: A transit planner's board asks how the 1848 Act shaped later reform. Which synthesis is best?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Rebuilding a capital under a military government
questions.learningObjective: Analyze a military motive for redesign
questions.stem: A transit planner's board asks why straight boulevards hindered barricades. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Barricades were banned by a separate law
options.misconception: introduces a legal cause not central

options.text: Wide straight streets denied cover and turning points
Narrow streets were simply dirtier
options.misconception: reduces a tactical choice to cleanliness

options.text: Residents refused to build barricades

questions.explanation: Straight, wide streets removed the cover and sharp turns that made barricades effective. Legal bans, cleanliness, or resident refusal are weaker explanations.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain a tariff advantage of empire
questions.stem: A transit planner's board asks how imperial preference aided manufacturers. Provide a model answer.

answer.exemplar: Imperial preference lowered or removed tariffs on goods traded within the empire, giving the metropole's manufacturers cheaper access to colonial consumers than foreign rivals had. This protected market share and stabilized demand.

questions.explanation: Preferential tariffs reduced costs for imperial goods in colonial markets. Foreign competitors faced higher barriers, so demand for domestic manufactures was protected.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why industry came first to Britain
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a source on British financial advantage

stimulus.body: London's capital markets financed canals, mines, and mills across the country, while continental lenders often favored state projects or land. British investors accepted higher risks for industrial ventures, and joint-stock companies spread those risks widely.

questions.stem: A transit planner's board reads this source. What does it best support?

options.text: Continental finance was more innovative
British finance was more willing to fund industry
Investors refused all industrial risk
Joint-stock companies were illegal in Britain

questions.explanation: The source shows British investors financing industrial ventures and spreading risk through joint-stock companies. It does not support continental superiority, risk refusal, or illegality.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a source on industrial research

stimulus.body: By 1910 the leading electrical firm employed over two hundred researchers and patented new lamp designs annually. Competitors without research staff relied on copying and fell behind in efficiency. Investors increasingly valued firms with in-house laboratories.

questions.stem: A transit planner's board reads this source. What does it best support?

options.text: Patents harmed industrial growth
Copying remained the best strategy
Researchers were unnecessary to success
In-house research became a competitive necessity

questions.explanation: The source shows research staff, patents, and investor preference for labs. It supports research as a necessity, not copying, dispensability, or patent harm.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the Act's preventive aim
questions.stem: A transit planner's board asks what the 1848 Act aimed to prevent. Provide a model answer.

answer.exemplar: The Act aimed to prevent epidemic disease by improving drainage, water supply, and street cleaning before outbreaks occurred. It shifted focus from treating the sick to removing the environmental causes of illness.

questions.explanation: Preventive sanitation targeted drainage, water, and cleanliness. The shift was from cure to prevention of environmental causes.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Rebuilding a capital under a military government
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a source on reconstruction outcomes

stimulus.body: The reconstruction replaced dense slums with broad avenues and public parks. Mortality declined in the rebuilt districts, yet rents rose and former residents moved to peripheral shantytowns. The project thus improved health metrics while worsening housing access for the poor.

questions.stem: A transit planner's board reads this source. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Mortality rose in rebuilt districts
The poor benefited equally from reconstruction
Health improved but housing access worsened for the poor
Rents fell for all residents

questions.explanation: The source records lower mortality alongside rising rents and peripheral displacement. It supports health gains with housing losses, not equal benefit or rising mortality.
